simulations.brief: A job posting asks for a 'cyber ninja rockstar' with no work role, no KSAs, and a CISSP requirement for a junior SOC job. Fix it.
simulations.debrief: NICE-based postings name the work role, list the KSAs, and match the cert to the level. 'Ninja rockstar' postings attract nobody qualified and repel everybody else.

evidence: Wanted: cyber ninja rockstar. Requirements: CISSP. Level: junior SOC analyst.
Junior SOC maps to Cyber Defense Analyst; CISSP is a senior-level cert.
steps.explain: The cert does not match the level, and there is no work role or KSA list. Candidates cannot self-select and hiring cannot screen.
options: Rewrite with the Cyber Defense Analyst work role, KSAs, and a junior-appropriate cert
Keep the posting; ninjas will apply
steps.symptom: A posting with no work role and a mismatched cert requirement.

evidence: KSAs: knowledge of SIEM queries; skill in triage; ability to follow playbooks.
steps.explain: Concrete KSAs let candidates self-assess and let interviewers test. Vague postings produce vague hires.

sections.heading: Framework Structure
items: Framework purpose — NIST SP 800-181's NICE Framework is a descriptive reference, not a certification: it organizes cybersecurity work into categories, specialty areas, and work roles, each with defined tasks and KSAs.

Work roles — the hierarchy refines: categories (broad mission areas) contain specialty areas (focused functions), which contain work roles (specific groupings of work), each defined by tasks and the knowledge, skills, and abilities to perform them.
Seven — Securely Provision, Operate and Maintain, Oversee and Govern, Protect and Defend, Analyze, Collect and Operate, Investigate.
Framework scope — titles vary; the work is what the framework standardizes. (This bootcamp adds a 'Framework Structure' domain on top for the meta-concepts.).
Common trap — categories contain work roles which contain KSAs.
Skipping the key question — does the NICE Framework test people, or describe work.
Skipping the key question — if two companies call the same work by different titles, what lets you compare them.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

sections.heading: Securely Provision
items: Securely Provision covers the builders — system architects, secure software developers, and everyone whose decisions shape system security before deployment. 'Provision' includes proving.

Security architecture — test and evaluation is the category's verification arm: security assessments, code review, and requirements validation proving the system as built meets its security requirements.
Test and evaluation — provisioning includes acquiring: secure integration, vendor security evaluation, and supply-chain risk management.
Common trap — provision first, assess risk later.
Skipping the key question — when is security cheapest to build in — during design, or after deployment.
Skipping the key question — what eliminates a vulnerability class entirely, versus finding instances of it.

sections.heading: Operate & Maintain
items: Sustainment — operate and Maintain is the sustainment backbone: administration, maintenance, and support of systems, networks, and data — the daily work that keeps security controls functioning. The category treats sustainment as a discipline with KSAs, not as the absenc…

Secure administration — least privilege, change control, configuration baselines, and vigilance — is a security discipline, not just an ops one. The category places data administration here because day-to-day data operations — grants, backups, monitoring — are security controls in…

Admin KSAs — the category's KSAs reflect that admin work is privileged work, with attacker-grade consequences for failure. With the right KSAs (recognizing security-relevant symptoms, proper escalation, secure troubleshooting), the helpdesk becomes a detection sensor, n…
Lifecycle — sustainment is active: patching, configuration review, capacity planning, and documentation updates across the lifecycle.
Technical support — the category includes support because user-facing operations surface what monitoring misses.
Common trap — support staff shouldn't touch security.
Common trap — data security is the app team's job.
Common trap — operations don't need security KSAs.
Common trap — admins don't need security training.

sections.heading: Oversee & Govern
items: Oversee and Govern is the leadership category — strategy, policy, risk management, legal/privacy guidance, and program advocacy.
Policy — someone must decide risk appetite, fund the program, and set policy — that's governance work with its own KSAs (not just 'management experience').
Strategy — the category's strategy work keeps the program aimed at the mission, not at the latest tool.
Risk management's job is decision support, not veto — assess the risk, present options with trade-offs, and let accountable leaders accept, mitigate, or avoid it.
Risk decisions — the category frames risk work as mission enablement — the organization takes risks constantly; governance makes them explicit and managed.
Common trap — risk registers are the whole job.
Common trap — legal only gets involved after a breach.

sections.heading: Protect & Defend
items: Protect and Defend scope — the category unifies around the mission: defend internal systems and networks.
Incident — Incident response spans preparation (playbooks, tooling, training), detection and analysis, containment/eradication/recovery, and post-incident learning.
Lifecycle — the work role's KSAs cover the full lifecycle — that's what makes responders effective under pressure.

Vulnerability assessment — control assessment (testing whether controls work, not just whether they exist) catches the gap between documented and actual security. Assessment's defensive value is in the analysis: which weaknesses matter (exploitability × exposure × asset value), what…
Common trap — intel analysts don't need defender input.
Common trap — only technical controls need assessment.
Common trap — assessors don't need attacker thinking.
Common trap — audits are annual so controls are fine.

sections.heading: More core topics
items: Analyze is the evaluation layer — reviewing threat, vulnerability, and target information to judge its meaning and usefulness for intelligence.

Intelligence requirements — the questions stakeholders need answered — focus both analysis and collection. Targets analysis studies what adversaries value and intend — which lets defenders prioritize: the assets adversaries actually pursue get the strongest protection.
Direction — the category's discipline starts with direction: know the question before you evaluate the data.

Analytic confidence — aggregation collects; analysis concludes — with confidence levels, gaps, and implications. Professional analysis expresses uncertainty explicitly: high/moderate/low confidence, key assumptions, and conflicting evidence shown — not hidden.
Integrity under pressure — is the category's core ethic.
Common trap — exploitation analysis is offensive work.
Common trap — targets analysis is targeting people.
Common trap — analysts don't need technical depth.
Common trap — collection doesn't need analysts.

Coordination — operational planning deconflicts, sequences, and resources the effort: objectives, authorized methods, coordination with stakeholders, and risk controls. Coordination — shared requirements, deconfliction, handoff discipline — multiplies effectiveness.
